# Capacity Prior to Access — AI in Early Childhood Education

> Markdown (GEO/AEO) version of <https://mauricio.issei.com.br/en/capacidade-antes-do-acesso>. Author: **Mauricio Yokoyama Issei** · en-BR · Published: 2026-08-27 · Updated: 2026-08-27.

## In short

Responsible integration of the AI in the founding years **is not a function of child access to technology**, but the interaction between developmental readiness, adult competence, mediation quality, institutional governance and cognitive function attributed to AI in the activity. *Capacity-before-access* is presented here as **analytical proposition derived from policy comparison** — not as a principle already enshrined in the literature.

- **Two domains, not one** — Children's education (0–6) and initial Fundamental (~6–13) are not generalised; confusing them invalidates the conclusion.
- **Four layers of competence** — capacity, judgment, mediation and governance; literature almost always measures only the first, and by self-perception.
- **Required, not enough** — P1 is partially sustainable, P2 is not supported by any revised study, P3 (conditionality) is the strongest.
- **Replacement × magnification** — with unrestricted access, − 17% in the final test without AI; with pedagogic guardrails, sustained gain (Bastani et al., 2025, PNAS).

## The unit of analysis

The relevant unit is not the child dyad + AI, but the adult system + mediation + technology + child + institutional context. This explains why two rooms using exactly the same tool produce opposite results: when the child asks, the AI answers and the child copies, the cognitive function of the tool is to replace; when the teacher proposes the problem, the child formulates, the AI offers a counterexample and the teacher questions the reasoning, the function is to expand. The relevant variable is not whether AI was used, but what cognitive function it performed.

## The three governance architectures

The informational comparison is not the binary pair prohibition–capacitation, but three models: age restriction (chronological age as main safeguard, case of UNESCO recommendation of 13 years); capacity conditioned access (age + previous teaching competence + gradual introduction, Norwegian case for the 8th–10th year); and unrestricted market-oriented access (technological availability as determinant, case of commercial adoption without policy mediation). The productive question is which architecture best corresponds to the risk, developmental maturity and mediation capacity of each context.

## What the article does not conclude

It does not conclude that AI should be used with children, nor that it should be prohibited. It concludes on conditional governance architecture, whose predictive validity remains open. The stated limitation is the absence of longitudinal and experimental studies linking teaching competence, quality of mediation and infant outcomes specifically with AI in the two age-old domains, and every statement of the article is calibrated by this absence. The restriction appears as a transitional governance mechanism while the capacity is not established, not as a mandatory previous step in the whole context.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What does "capacity before access" mean?**

It is the proposition that children's access to the generative AI should be conditioned to the available mediation capacity — adult competence, quality of pedagogical intervention and institutional safeguards — and not just chronological age. The article treats it as an analytical proposition derived from the comparison between political architectures, not as a principle already established by the literature or by any current policy.

**Why separate early childhood education from elementary school?**

Because they are distinct domains and the evidence of one does not transfer to the other. Early childhood education (ECEC) designates 0 to 6 years, before compulsory schooling, where the direct use of the tool by the child is minimal and the focus is on adult education. The initial Fundamental (about 6 to 13 years) is where Norway published official guidelines per school stage in 2026, and where the child is already in literacy and numeration. Treating them as a single block compromises the validity of inference, because the evidence of one domain does not support conclusions about the other.

**What are the four layers of adult competence?**

Capability (the teacher knows how the tool works), judgment (knows how to decide when to use, when not to use and for what purpose), mediation (knows how to intervene during use — question, verify, withdraw support) and governance (the institution allows and structure this intervention, with time, infrastructure and policy). Most of the literature measures only the first, in general by self-perception, silencing precisely the layers that the strongest evidence suggests are decisive.

**When does cognitive discharge become a replacement?**

Unloading operational load can be desirable and release capacity for higher order reasoning; the precise question is when offloading becomes a replacement for the cognitive process that the child needs to develop. In the randomized trial by Bastani et al. (2025), unrestricted access to the model improved 48% performance during practice but produced a result 17% lower than the control in the final test without AI; with guardrails that prohibited delivering the final response, the improvement was 127% and the gain remained.

**Does the restriction of smartphones serve as evidence of a generative AI?**

Not directly. The risk mechanisms are distinct: smartphone and social networks operate on attention, distraction and social comparison, while generativa AI operates on cognitive production, outsourcing of reasoning and writing. Evidence of device restriction is treated as comparative evidence of policy — useful for understanding how institutional restrictions behave — rather than as causal evidence of AI.

**What does the Norwegian policy of 2026 show?**

Demonstrates policy design (policy design): a coherent architecture that combines minimum age, previous teaching competence and explicit pedagogical purpose, with almost total restriction between 6 and 13 years and gradual use between 14 and 16 conditioned to teacher competence. It does not demonstrate policy effectiveness (policy effectiveness): it is too recent for longitudinal impact assessment, and no policy in itself constitutes an experiment.

**Is teacher training enough to integrate AI with responsibility?**

Not according to the literature reviewed. No study supports the sufficiency of teaching competence as an isolated variable, and the I AI Act itself rejects this premise implicitly by requiring institutional supervision for high-risk uses, regardless of the individual competence of the educator. Adult competence is probably a necessary enabling condition; the most likely intermediate variable is the quality of pedagogical mediation.

## Glossary

- **Capacity before access** — Proposal to condition access to available mediation capacity, not only to chronological age.
- **Domain A (ECEC)** — Children's education, 0–6 years: the focus is on adult competence, upstream of any direct use.
- **Domain B (initial Foundation)** — Early years, ~6–13: where restriction, conditioned introduction and mediation affect the use by the child.
- **Educational mediation** — Adult intervention during use — question, verify and withdraw support progressively.
- **Cognitive replacement** — When the tool performs the cognitive process that the child would need to develop for itself.
- **Pedagogical guardians** — Drawing restrictions that prevent the AI from delivering the final response, converting substitution into scaffold.
- **Policy design × policy effectiveness** — Consistent design of a policy is not proof that it produces better outcomes: a policy is not an experiment.
